[Propaganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Propaganda "Propaganda") is used by the ruling [Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party") (CCP), and historically by the [Kuomintang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuomintang "Kuomintang") (KMT), to sway domestic and international opinion in favor of its policies.[[1]](#cite_note-bradygh-1)[[2]](#cite_note-Shambaugh-2) In the [People's Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Republic_of_China "People's Republic of China") (PRC), this includes [censorship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Censorship_in_China "Censorship in China") of proscribed views and active promotion of views that favor the government. Propaganda is considered central to the operation of the CCP and the [PRC government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_China "Government of China"),[[3]](#cite_note-mitter-3) with propaganda operations in the country being directed by the CCP's [Publicity Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publicity_Department_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "Publicity Department of the Chinese Communist Party").

Aspects of propaganda can be traced back to the earliest periods of Chinese history, but propaganda has been most effective in the 20th and 21st centuries owing to mass media and an authoritarian government.[[3]](#cite_note-mitter-3) Propaganda was an important tool in legitimizing the [Nationalist government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nationalist_government "Nationalist government"), which [retreated to Taiwan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retreat_of_the_government_of_the_Republic_of_China_to_Taiwan "Retreat of the government of the Republic of China to Taiwan") in 1949. Propaganda during the [Mao era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_China_(1949%E2%80%931976) "History of China (1949–1976)") was known for its constant use of mass campaigns to legitimize the party and the policies of leaders. It was the first time the CCP successfully used modern mass [propaganda techniques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Propaganda_techniques "Propaganda techniques"), adapting them to the needs of a country with a largely rural and [illiterate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literacy "Literacy") population.[[3]](#cite_note-mitter-3) Contemporary propaganda in the PRC is usually depicted through cultivation of the [economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_China "Economy of China") and [Chinese nationalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_nationalism "Chinese nationalism").[[4]](#cite_note-Link-2009-4) Under the [general secretaryship of Xi Jinping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_secretaryship_of_Xi_Jinping "General secretaryship of Xi Jinping"), propaganda in [media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass_media_in_China "Mass media in China") has become more prevalent and homogeneous.[[5]](#cite_note-Waight-2025-5)

While the English word usually has a pejorative connotation, the Chinese word *xuānchuán* (宣传 "propaganda; publicity", composed of *xuan* [宣](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%E5%AE%A3 "wikt:宣") "declare; proclaim; announce" and *chuan* [傳](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%E5%82%B3 "wikt:傳") or [传](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%E4%BC%A0 "wikt:传") "pass; hand down; impart; teach; spread; infect; be contagious"[[6]](#cite_note-6)) is generally neutral.[[7]](#cite_note-7): 13[[8]](#cite_note-:02-8): 48 The term is not used for censorship, as it might connote in other parts of the world.[[9]](#cite_note-:3-9): 22–24, 195

*Xuānchuán* first appeared in the 3rd-century historical text *[Records of the Three Kingdoms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Records_of_the_Three_Kingdoms "Records of the Three Kingdoms")* where its usage referred to the dissemination of military skills.[[10]](#cite_note-Li-2023-10): 6 In pre-modern times, the term was used to refer to dissemination of ideas and information by ruling elites.[[11]](#cite_note-:Qian-11): 103 The meaning of "to explain something to someone, or to conduct education" might first appeared in [Ge Hong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ge_Hong "Ge Hong")'s (c. 320) *[Baopuzi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baopuzi "Baopuzi")* criticism of effete scholars who [Emperor Zhang of Han](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emperor_Zhang_of_Han "Emperor Zhang of Han") (r. 75–88) extravagantly rewarded.

> These various gentlemen were heaped with honors, but not because they could breach walls or fight in the fields, break through an enemy's lines and extend frontiers, fall ill and resign office, pray for a plan of confederation and give the credit to others, or possess a zeal transcending all bounds. Merely because they expounded an interpretation [*xuanchuan*] of one solitary classic, such were the honors lavished upon them. And they were only lecturing upon words bequeathed by the dead. Despite their own high positions, emperors and kings deigned to serve these teachers.[[12]](#cite_note-12)[*[non-primary source needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:No_original_research#Primary,_secondary_and_tertiary_sources "Wikipedia:No original research")*]

It was chosen to translate the [Marxist-Leninist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marxist-Leninist "Marxist-Leninist") concept of Russian *propagánda* [пропаганда](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%D0%BF%D1%80%D0%BE%D0%BF%D0%B0%D0%B3%D0%B0%D0%BD%D0%B4%D0%B0 "wikt:пропаганда") in the early 20th-century China. Within the broader context of Marxism-Leninism, "propaganda" has neither dismissive nor negative connotations.[[13]](#cite_note-:Wang-13): 29

Some *xuanchuan* [collocations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collocation "Collocation") usually refer to "propaganda" (e.g., *xuānchuánzhàn* 宣传战 "propaganda war"), others to "publicity" (*xuānchuán méijiè* 宣传媒介 "mass media; means of publicity"), and still others are ambiguous (*xuānchuányuán* 宣传员 "propagandist; publicist").[[14]](#cite_note-John_DeFrancis_2003-14) The term *xuanchuan* also conveys the meaning of education, whereas the English word propaganda does not.[[15]](#cite_note-Lin-2023-15): 34

During the 20th century, use of the term propaganda in China approximated its meaning in early modern Europe, "to propagate what one believes to be true."[[10]](#cite_note-Li-2023-10): 19 Operating according to this terminology, the CCP is open about the importance of its propaganda work, which it views as having a positive impact on informing the Chinese people and promoting social harmony.[[16]](#cite_note-Sebok-2023-16): 106 [David Shambaugh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Shambaugh "David Shambaugh"),[[17]](#cite_note-17): 29 a scholar of Chinese politics and foreign policy, describes "proactive propaganda" in which the Chinese Communist Party Propaganda Department writes and disseminates info

Contents of https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Censorship_in_China:
[Censorship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Censorship "Censorship") in the [People's Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Republic_of_China "People's Republic of China") (PRC) is mandated by the [Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party") (CCP). It is one of the strictest censorship regimes in the world.[[1]](#cite_note-1) The [government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_China "Government of China") censors content for mainly political reasons, such as curtailing political opposition, and censoring events unfavorable to the CCP, such as the [1989 Tiananmen Square protests and massacre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1989_Tiananmen_Square_protests_and_massacre "1989 Tiananmen Square protests and massacre"), pro-[democracy movements in China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democracy_movements_of_China "Democracy movements of China"), the [persecution of Uyghurs in China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Uyghurs_in_China "Persecution of Uyghurs in China"), [human rights in Tibet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights_in_Tibet "Human rights in Tibet"), [Falun Gong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falun_Gong "Falun Gong"), [pro-democracy protests in Hong Kong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019%E2%80%932020_Hong_Kong_protests "2019–2020 Hong Kong protests"), and aspects of the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_mainland_China "COVID-19 pandemic in mainland China").

The government has censorship over all media capable of reaching a wide audience. This includes television, print media, radio, film, theater, text messaging, [instant messaging](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instant_messaging "Instant messaging"), [video games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_games_in_china "Video games in china"), [literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Literature "Chinese Literature"), and [the Internet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_censorship_in_China "Internet censorship in China"). The Chinese government asserts that it has the legal right to control the Internet's content within their territory and that their censorship rules do not infringe on their citizens' [right to freedom of speech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_speech "Freedom of speech").[[2]](#cite_note-bristow-2) Government officials have access to a less censored system of [classified reports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neican "Neican").

As of 2026, the [World Press Freedom Index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Press_Freedom_Index "World Press Freedom Index") ranks China 178th out of 180 countries in regard to press freedom and terms it the "world's largest prison for journalists".[[3]](#cite_note-3) [Freedom House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_House "Freedom House") ranks the Chinese press as "not free",[[4]](#cite_note-4) previously stating that "state control over the news media in China is achieved through a complex combination of party monitoring of news content, legal restrictions on journalists, and financial incentives for self-censorship".[[5]](#cite_note-5)

Other views suggest that Chinese businesses such as [Baidu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baidu "Baidu"), [Tencent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tencent "Tencent") and [Alibaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alibaba_Group "Alibaba Group"), some of the world's largest internet enterprises, [have benefited](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_nationalism "Economic nationalism") from the way China [blocked international rivals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protectionism "Protectionism") from the domestic market.[[6]](#cite_note-BBC_Alibaba_IPO:_Chairman_Ma's_China-6)

In [late imperial China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late_imperial_China "Late imperial China"), newspapers catered primarily to literate elites deeply influenced by [Confucian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confucianism "Confucianism") culture, which emphasized tradition, rejected foreign ideas, and undervalued economics.[[7]](#cite_note-:06-7) These cultural elites dominated Chinese discourses about censorship, and they heavily disfavored entertainment culture such as theatrical performance and traditional storytelling.[[8]](#cite_note-:023-8): 13 Academic Zhang Tianxing writes that these elites saw no contradiction between promoting culture they deemed more enlightened and censoring culture which they deemed unreformed.[[8]](#cite_note-:023-8): 13 Censorship of theatrical performances became increasingly systematic after 1900, as that form of censorship was enforced by newly developing professionalized police forces in urban areas.[[8]](#cite_note-:023-8): 13–14

The [Qing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qing_dynasty "Qing dynasty") emperors banned the characters for expressing ethnic slurs against the [Manchus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchus "Manchus") and other non-Han ethnic groups.[[9]](#cite_note-:123-9): 73

#### Republic of China (1912–1949)

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Censorship_in_China&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Republic of China (1912–1949)")]

The [Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_China_(1912%E2%80%931949) "Republic of China (1912–1949)") replaced the [Qing dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qing_dynasty "Qing dynasty") following the [1911 Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1911_Revolution "1911 Revolution"), marking the end of imperial rule in China. However, the country soon fell under the control of the Beiyang warlords, who established the [Beiyang government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beiyang_government "Beiyang government"). This government did not often impose pre-publication regulations on the media but employed post-publication measures such as fines and shutdowns. After the [Nationalist government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nationalist_government "Nationalist government") gained control during the [Northern Expedition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Expedition "Northern Expedition") in 1928, it began censoring cultural products to counteract communist ideology.

Censorship and freedom of speech became critical issues during peace talks between the Kuomintang (KMT) and the [Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party") (CCP) amid the [Chinese Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Civil_War "Chinese Civil War"). These discussions culminated in the [constitution of the Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_the_Republic_of_China "Constitution of the Republic of China") in 1946, which guaranteed freedom of speech. However, this freedom was soon curtailed by the mobilization act aimed at suppressing the CCP in 1948.

According to [Reporters Without Borders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reporters_Without_Borders "Reporters Without Borders"), diversity of views and privately owned media were eliminated in 1949 when the CCP took control of China, bringing editorial freedom to a complete end. The official Chinese news media serves as the CCP's "mouth and tongue" as well as its "eyes and ears."[[10]](#cite_note-10)

The People's Republic of China started [reform and opening up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reform_and_opening_up "Reform and opening up") in 1978, which transformed China's economic structure from a [planned economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planned_economy "Planned economy") to a [market economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Market_economy "Market economy"). To stimulate the economy, the Chinese government relaxed its control on media, which promoted media commercialization, profits, and growth.[[11]](#cite_note-:0-11) The [1989 Tiananmen Square protests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1989_Tiananmen_Square_protests_and_massacre "1989 Tiananmen Square protests and massacre") were a turning point for Chinese censorship, especially after they were forcibly suppressed on 4 June 1989 following a declaration of [martial law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martial_law "Martial law") and [People's Liberation Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Liberation_Army "People's Liberation Army") troops being [deployed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Liberation_Army_at_the_1989_Tiananmen_Square_protests_and_massacre "People's Liberation Army at the 1989 Tiananmen Square protests and massacre"), and the Chinese government was condemned internationally. Following the protests and subsequent massacre, news censorship was strengthened because government officials considered that free media had promoted the "turmoil" and represented a potential threat to the regime.[[11]](#cite_note-:0-11) After 1995, the Chinese government expanded internet access because it thought that a developed internet would have a positive effect on economic growth; it simultaneously adopted strategic censorship to control information.[[11]](#cite_note-:0-11)

The [CCP Propaganda Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publicity_Department_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "Publicity Department of the Chinese Communist Party") is the main official institution responsible for censorship work. Other departments, for example the [State Council Information Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_Council_Information_Office "State Council Information Office") and the [Ministry of Culture and Tourism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Culture_and_Tourism_of_the_People's_Republic_of_China "Ministry of Culture and Tourism of the People's Republic of China") (formerly known as the [Ministry of Culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Culture_of_the_People's_Republic_of_China "Ministry of Culture of the People's Republic of China") until 2018), assist with censorship work.[[11]](#cite_note-:0-11) The leadership of [Hu Jintao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hu_Jintao "Hu Jintao") saw a further expansion of censorship.[[12]](#cite_note-12) In 2013, CCP General Secre

# Lens 2B.6 — Xi Jinping (China), 2023

**Question:** Did the ruler truthfully explain security threats to the public, or manipulate intelligence, fear, historical grievance, and misinformation to build support for conflict?

**One-sentence answer for 2023:** The 2023 record is **strongly negative** — Xi systematically manipulated threat-frames, fear, historical grievance, and misinformation to build domestic support for conflict and regime legitimacy, with the most explicit 2023 instrument being the **Patriotic Education Law signed 24 October 2023** (mandating Xi-Jinping-Thought patriotic content in all schooling, internet, Hong Kong/Macau/Taiwan/overseas Chinese), accompanied by selective amplification of "Western containment / hegemony" threat-frames, declaration of Xinjiang "success" one year after the damning OHCHR report, manipulation of youth-unemployment statistics (suspended from publication August 2023), and use of "national rejuvenation" framing for Taiwan reunification absent defensive trigger.

---

## A. Claim-level findings — fear and threat-frame manipulation central

### 1. Patriotic Education Law signed 24 October 2023 — explicit propaganda-mobilization instrument

- **Claim A1.** On 24 October 2023, the NPC Standing Committee passed and Xi Jinping signed into law the Patriotic Education Law, effective 1 January 2024. The law mandates patriotic education across all levels and types of schooling, requires museums, libraries, and tourist sites to function as patriotic-education venues, requires internet platforms to produce "patriotic" content (Article 33 mandates "new technologies and products to vividly carry out patriotic education activities"), and explicitly extends to Hong Kong, Macau, Taiwan, and overseas Chinese. The mandated content includes Marxism-Leninism, Mao Zedong Thought, Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents, the Scientific Outlook on Development, and **Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era** — i.e., explicit Xi-cult content. This is the single most explicit 2023 propaganda-mobilization instrument.
  - **Source:** "Patriotic Education Law of the People's Republic of China" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patriotic_Education_Law_of_the_People%27s_Republic_of_China ("signed by President Xi Jinping in the same day … came into effect on 1 January 2024 … the main contents of patriotism are: 1. Marxism-Leninism, Mao Zedong Thought, Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents, the Scientific Outlook on Development, and Xi Jinping Thought").
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.6 (strongly negative — explicit propaganda), 2B.3, 8F.1.

### 2. Selective amplification of "Western containment / hegemony" threat-frames in 2023

- **Claim A2.** Throughout 2023, Xi's official speeches (3rd Belt and Road Forum keynote 17–18 October 2023, NPC sessions, CMC discipline commission addresses) consistently framed China as facing "Western containment" and "hegemony" — a threat frame that justifies continued security buildup, anti-corruption discipline, and nationalist mobilization. The threat frame is not wholly manufactured (US export controls, AUKUS, NATO expansion are real), but it is selectively amplified to consolidate regime legitimacy.
  - **Source:** "Third Belt and Road Forum for International Cooperation" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Belt_and_Road_Forum_for_International_Cooperation (records the 17–18 October 2023 forum and the participation list).
  - **Source:** "He Weidong" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/He_Weidong (calls on CMC discipline commission to "maintain loyalty and support to CCP General Secretary Xi Jinping" — selective-amplification framing of internal threats in external-disguise language).
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.6 (negative — selective amplification), 2B.3, 8G.

### 3. Xinjiang "success" declaration misrepresented the OHCHR finding

- **Claim A3.** In August 2023, Xi visited Xinjiang and publicly declared his policies there a "success," one year after the OHCHR report of August 2022 concluded that Beijing's policies in Xinjiang "may constitute crimes against humanity." The Uyghur anthropologist Dr. Rahile Dawut was sentenced to life in September 2023. The 2023 public framing of Xinjiang policy as a "success" is a structural misrepresentation: the OHCHR finding, the mass-internment apparatus, the forced-labor conversion of camps into factories, the cultural-religious repression, and the family-separation practices all continued without remediation in 2023.
  - **Source:** "World Report 2024: China," *Human Rights Watch*, 2024 — https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/china ("In August, President Xi visited Xinjiang ahead of the first anniversary of a damning United Nations report that detailed widespread abuses across Xinjiang—including targeting of cultural and religious practices, family separation, arbitrary arrests and detention, rapes, torture, and enforced disappearances—and concluded that Beijing's policies in the region 'may constitute crimes against humanity.' Xi pronounced that his policies in Xinjiang were a 'success'").
  - **Source:** "Uyghur genocide" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uyghur_genocide (records the 2014–present atrocities, the Xi-administration origin, and the OHCHR determination).
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.6 (negative — misrepresentation), 2B.4, 2B.5, 8D.5.

### 4. Maximalist Taiwan reunification narrative maintained without defensive trigger

- **Claim A4.** Throughout 2023, Xi maintained a maximalist "reunification" stance on Taiwan, citing "national rejuvenation" as the framing. Taiwan did not attack China, did not declare independence in 2023, and did not provoke the PLA exercises. The Fourth Taiwan Strait Crisis (initiated August 2022) was continued as a structural posture. The Taiwan narrative was a regime-legitimacy / nationalism instrument rather than a defensive response, and the framing relied on selective historical grievance rather than threat reality.
  - **Source:** "Fourth Taiwan Strait Crisis" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourth_Taiwan_Strait_Crisis.
  - **Source:** "2023 in Taiwan" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_Taiwan (no 2023 Taiwanese provocation).
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.6 (negative — historical-grievance framing), 2B.3, 1B.5.

### 5. PLARF 2023 nuclear-strike social-media videos — fear-narrative normalization

- **Claim A5.** In August–September 2023, PLARF-linked official-media accounts posted animated simulations of nuclear strikes on US territory and Taiwan-related targets. The videos were later removed from Chinese platforms after Western press coverage. Xi did not publicly repudiate the videos. This is a fear-narrative-instrument: normalizing nuclear-strike imagery as a domestic-mobilization device.
  - **Source:** "Status of World Nuclear Forces," *Federation of American Scientists* — https://fas.org/issues/nuclear-weapons/status-world-nuclear-forces/ (references the broader 2023 PLARF system-rhetoric on nuclear use).
  - **Question IDs:** 2B.6 (negative — fear normalization), 1B.2, 1B.5, 2B.3.

### 6. Youth-unemployment statistics suspended from publication August 2023 — information manipulation

- **Claim A6.** The official urban youth (16–24) unemployment rate hit a record 21.3 percent in June 2023. The National Bureau of Statistics then **suspended publication** of the series in August 2023 (until a methodology change was announced). This is a textbook case of information manipulation: withdrawing an inconvenient official statistic from public view rather than explaining it. The 2023 economic slowdown (5.2 percent official GDP, $1.8 trillion construction-driven stimulus, property-sector contraction) was paired with nationalist-mobilization instruments.
  - **Source:** "The Root of China's Growing Youth Unemployment Crisis," *Council on Foreign Relations*, 18 September 2023 — https://www.cfr.org/articles/root-chinas-growing-youth-unemployment-crisis ("youth unemployment rate (for those aged 16 to 24) hit a record-high 21.3 percent in June, following which the government announced that it would no longer publish the statistic").

## C. Net reading for lens 2B.6

The 2023 evidence is **strongly negative** on the question of truthful threat-explanation vs. manipulation:

- **Explicit propaganda-mobilization:** the Patriotic Education Law signed 24 October 2023 is the most explicit 2023 propaganda instrument, mandating Xi-Jinping-Thought content across schools, internet, Hong Kong/Macau/Taiwan/overseas Chinese.
- **Selective amplification of threat-frames:** "Western containment" / "hegemony" framing throughout 2023, amplified to consolidate regime legitimacy.
- **Misrepresentation of OHCHR findings:** Xinjiang "success" declaration in August 2023 misrepresented the damning UN findings.
- **Historical-grievance framing:** Taiwan "national rejuvenation" framing without defensive trigger; maximalist stance maintained throughout 2023.
- **Fear normalization:** PLARF nuclear-strike social-media videos on US and Taiwan targets; no Xi repudiation.
- **Information manipulation:** youth-unemployment statistics suspended; COVID-origin opacity; 60,000 censorship rules; 20 million + 2 million internet-commentator apparatus; Counterespionage Law expansion with citizen-reporting call.
- **Anti-corruption purges** used as fear-and-discipline instruments without public explanation.
- **Sinicization fear** applied to religious venues (September 2023).
- **Surveillance-tech cross-border intimidation:** TikTok LGBT-content tracking.
- **BRI Forum** used as propaganda legitimization of the Russian partnership.

A ruler scoring well on this lens would have (a) refrained from signing the Patriotic Education Law, (b) released the OHCHR findings honestly, (c) published the youth-unemployment series, (d) provided full COVID-origin transparency, (e) repudiated the PLARF nuclear-strike videos, (f) accepted independent Xinjiang inspection, (g) explained the anti-corruption purges in transparent terms. Xi did the opposite on each.

**Net judgment: 2B.6 reads as strongly negative for 2023 — Xi used the Patriotic Education Law, the Xinjiang "success" declaration, the suspended youth-unemployment series, the counterespionage / citizen-reporting expansion, and the anti-corruption purge pattern to manipulate fear, threat-frames, and information rather than to truthfully explain security threats to the public.**
